title: Shortest Cycle in a Graph
statement:
An undirected graph has `n` vertices numbered `0` to `n - 1`. Each entry `edges[i] = [u, v]` joins vertices `u` and `v`. No edge joins a vertex to itself, and any two vertices share at most one edge.

A cycle is a walk that begins and ends at the same vertex and never uses any edge more than once; its length is the number of edges it uses. Return the length of the shortest cycle in the graph, or `-1` if the graph has no cycle at all.
notes:
## Intuition

A simple check is to remove each edge `(a, b)` in turn and find the shortest path from `a` to `b` without it; that path plus the edge is the shortest cycle through that edge. That repeats a BFS per edge. Instead, run one BFS from every vertex. In a BFS tree, an edge that leads to an already visited vertex (other than the vertex's own parent) closes a loop: walking down the tree to `node`, across the edge to `next`, and back up the tree has length `dist[node] + dist[next] + 1`. That walk always contains a cycle at most that long, and when the BFS starts on a shortest cycle it measures that cycle exactly, so the minimum over all starts is the answer.

## Approach

1. Build an adjacency list `graph`.
2. For each `start`, run BFS keeping `dist` (layer) and `parent` (tree parent) of every reached vertex.
3. When `node` sees an unvisited neighbour, give it `dist[node] + 1` and record `node` as its parent.
4. When it sees a visited neighbour that is not its parent, update `best` with `dist[node] + dist[next] + 1`.
5. Return `best`, or `-1` if it was never set.

## Example 1, step by step

From `start = 0`: vertices `1` and `2` both get `dist = 1` with parent `0`. Processing `1`, its neighbour `0` is its parent and is skipped, but `2` is already visited, so `best = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3`. The square `3-4-5-6` later gives `1 + 2 + 1 = 4` from `start = 3`, which does not beat `3`. The answer is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · (n + m)): one BFS per vertex.
- Space: O(n + m) for the graph and the per-BFS arrays.

## Pitfalls

- Skip only the edge back to the parent; any other visited neighbour, even in the same layer, closes a cycle (odd cycles are found this way).
- A single BFS from vertex `0` is not enough: the graph may be disconnected, and a BFS that does not start on the shortest cycle can overestimate it.
- The graph may contain isolated vertices and several components; return `-1` only when no start found a cycle.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `graph` | adjacency list of the undirected graph |
| `best` | shortest cycle length found so far |
| `start` | the vertex the current BFS starts from |
| `dist` | BFS distance from `start`, `-1` if not reached |
| `parent` | the vertex that discovered each vertex in this BFS |
| `queue`, `head` | BFS queue and the index of the next vertex to process |
| `node`, `next` | the vertex being processed and one of its neighbours |
